title: Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors
one_liner: Sell seed VCs, pharma BD teams and AI-bio founders confidential 'does this paper's key result actually work?' intelligence, from anonymous postdoc consensus polls up to paid replication of the one key experiment.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms, pharma BD and scouting teams evaluating academic spinouts or in-licensing, and AI-bio startups building on published wet-lab claims. Pay $4-6k for a poll-only memo and $15-40k for a key-experiment replication.
problem: Investors and BD teams can't tell which high-profile papers replicate. The truth exists as hallway consensus: 'that result only works in the first author's hands', 'nobody outside that lab can get the organoid protocol to run', 'cells were cultured as previously described' with four layers of citations. Formal diligence hires KOL consultants who are conflicted and often the PI's friends, or a CRO that needs 4 months and a full protocol. Bad academic-asset bets burn $5-20M before anyone notices.
solution: Wedge product 'Bench Pulse': in 5 business days, poll 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous postdocs and senior techs working in the exact subfield about the named claim, reagents and protocol. Deliver a structured memo with consensus, red flags, the Figure-3 problem, which reagents or lots are fragile, and a 'what to test first' plan. Upsell: 'Key-Figure Replication'. A pool of laid-off or between-position scientists runs the single decisive experiment in 3-4 weeks in rented bench space (not on university property), with pre-registered success criteria and blinded readout.
why_now: Biotech funding since 2023 rewards capital efficiency, so seed funds want cheaper, faster kill decisions. Pharma is shopping for early assets in academia and abroad. AI-bio companies are building on published wet-lab claims with little bench sense. NIH disruption and biotech layoffs have released a large pool of very good bench scientists who want paid, flexible work. Expert-network compliance norms are now well understood, so a compliant structure is feasible.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee per poll memo and per replication study. Annual retainer for funds that want a pipeline-wide 'bench pulse' (about $30-60k). Optional success-fee or advisory equity for AI-bio startups.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not lab capacity, it is candid consensus. Replication is expensive, but the postdoc informal network already knows which labs' results hold up. The winning move is to monetize that gossip compliantly and only spend on replication after the poll narrows the question. GLG-style expert calls fail because they interview one conflicted senior person instead of 10 juniors who actually do the pipetting.
first_30_days: Choose one subfield you personally have 20 contacts in (for example CAR-T, organoids, targeted protein degradation or spatial biology). Build the compliant NDA plus anonymity protocol with a lawyer for about $3k. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on one asset they are already looking at. Convert the fund that reacts to a paid $5k poll, then upsell one replication. Pay panelists $150-300 per poll from the first revenue.

title: Trust Oracle for Rental Listings and Agents
one_liner: An API that answers whether a vacation rental exists, is legally registered and is controlled by the host, so payment firms, insurers and AI booking agents can refuse scams.
customer: Payment providers handling travel, travel insurers, villa-rental agencies and AI trip-agent developers, later consumers via a plug-in.
problem: AI-generated photos and cloned listings fuel rental fraud, and agents will soon book unattended. The EU short-term rental regulation requires registration numbers from May 2026, but there is no cross-border way to verify them and each registry differs. Bans (Barcelona 2028, Palma) will also see illegal listings delisted at the last minute, stranding guests.
solution: Aggregate public registries (Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, France, NYC and others), geocode the address and match it to satellite and street imagery, reverse-search photos and detect duplicates. Return a verified, unverified or unregistered verdict with evidence in under two seconds, as an API and an agent tool.
why_now: Registry numbers make 'is it legal' a lookup for the first time, agentic booking needs automated trust, and AI imagery has broken manual checks. Enforcement is rising (Spain's USD 75M fine on Airbnb).
revenue_model: USD 0.05-0.50 per check, USD 2-10K per month enterprise plans, and a share of insurer premiums saved.
non_obvious_insight: Registration numbers convert legality from opinion into data, and agents cannot get a bad feeling about a listing. Whoever builds the legality and fraud graph first becomes infrastructure for every automated booking flow.
first_30_days: Build for Spain, Italy and Portugal using public registers. Offer a free check widget to villa agencies, and backtest known scam cases to pitch two travel-insurer fraud teams.

title: Savings Groups as Verified Human Endpoints for Agents
angle: AI agents & the agent economy x Emerging markets leapfrogging
one_liner: A group-guaranteed 'verify this physical fact' API, fulfilled by African savings groups and starting with solar and battery installations.
customer: Donor-funded energy-access results-based-financing programme administrators (who pay per verified installation), inverter and battery brands verifying warranties and distributor claims, and asset lenders and insurers. Agents that need physical facts are the long-term buyer.
problem: Agents can hire humans, but RentAHuman had about 590,000 sign-ups against about 11,300 active bounties and 5,500 completed jobs, plus scams and payment errors. Trusted agent demand is scarce because individual anonymous workers are a bad trust unit. Meanwhile Africa's distributed solar and battery boom (about 17 GW in 2026) is largely invisible: Ember's estimates are about 2x official statistics, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Lenders, insurers and utilities cannot verify what exists.
solution: A verify(system, location) API exposed as an MCP tool and payable by x402 or MPP. Fulfillment goes to savings groups (VSLAs and farmer groups), which already have joint-liability norms and a treasurer. Members capture device-attested photos, inverter-app screenshots, kWh readings and GPS. Random cross-checks by other members catch fraud, and a small bond from pooled savings backs each group. Payment goes to the group's mobile-money account, not to anonymous individuals.
why_now: The Hormuz energy shock and the solar and battery boom are pulling in subsidy programmes and lenders who need verification. Sandi AI shows 10,000+ farmer groups are already digitized in Uganda, Kenya and Tanzania. The public failure of agent-hiring marketplaces has created demand for a trust layer. Machine-payment protocols make per-task settlement cheap.
revenue_model: $4-8 per verification: about 65% to the group, 10% to the bond pool, 25% platform margin. Later, recurring data subscriptions on verified asset registries.
non_obvious_insight: Individuals are the wrong unit of trust for agent-issued work. A group with existing joint liability solves identity, fraud, payout and dispute in one move. Demand-first beats marketplace-first: RBF programmes already pay for verification today, so agents can be layered on afterwards.
first_30_days: Partner with an existing savings-group network (for example Sandi AI or a VSLA association) and onboard 20 groups in Uganda. Pitch one RBF administrator or battery distributor a 500-check pilot at $6 each. Run the verification workflow on WhatsApp and mobile money, with manual review of every submission.

title: License-in-a-Box for Insourcing Property Owners
one_liner: A licensed managing-broker entity, trust-account oversight and compliance layer that lets owners run AI-native property management in-house without building licensing state by state.
customer: Institutional owners, family offices, search-fund operators and AI-native property-ops startups with 500-10,000 units that want to insource management.
problem: Owners are insourcing to capture AI efficiency and stop paying a percentage-of-rent fee (T2 Capital's Base Living launched with 24 site associates and 8 corporate staff across three states). Most states require a licensed broker of record, trust accounts, fair-housing controls and E&O cover, and each new state costs months of licensing and hires.
solution: A licensed entity in 20+ states supervises the owner's own operation: trust-accounting oversight integrated with Yardi, AppFolio and Entrata, monthly reconciliations, fair-housing and fee-law compliance, E&O coverage and regulator liaison. Owners run day-to-day operations with their own AI stack.
why_now: The insourcing wave is underway, third-party manager incentives are misaligned, and the fee and pricing-law patchwork is raising compliance load.
revenue_model: $1.50-3.50 per unit per month plus a $10-25K onboarding fee per state, and an E&O program revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier to AI-native operations is not software but a licensed human of record in every state, which is cheap to rent and expensive to build. Incumbent managers will not sell it because it undermines their fee model.
first_30_days: Form the entity with a multi-state-licensed broker and counsel. Sign two owners with 500-2,000 units in one or two states as reduced-rate design partners. Get an E&O quote and publish a free state-by-state licensing matrix as a lead magnet.

title: Pickleball Courts Inside Empty Fellowship Halls
one_liner: A turnkey operator that converts congregations' idle gyms and fellowship halls into revenue-sharing indoor pickleball venues, with lines, nets, insurance and booking handled.
customer: Congregations (churches, synagogues, mosques, temples) with a gym or hall and parking lot, who receive a rent share. Players (often retirees on weekday mornings) pay $8-15 per session.
problem: US pickleball grew from 13.6M (2023) to 24.3M (2025) players, but courts are scarce (about 1 dedicated court per 1,000 participants in the Mid-Atlantic, and about $900M of investment needed per a 2022 SFIA report). Outdoor courts are being restricted or closed by noise complaints. Meanwhile congregations that are shrinking or flat (only 33% of Americans attend monthly) sit on large rooms used a few hours a week, and fear liability and tax surprises.
solution: A standard hall kit (removable court lines, portable nets, wall padding, ball machine), a legal and insurance package (lease template, additional-insured wording, a flat-rent structure designed to avoid UBIT problems, waivers), a booking app with open-play scheduling and rating-linked sessions, and part-time paid hosts. Indoor play removes the neighbor-noise problem.
why_now: Participation more than doubled in two years, and noise fights are closing outdoor courts (Kirkwood MO, Walnut Creek CA, Halifax). Church rental-liability gaps are a known insurance pain point. Congregations need non-donation income.
revenue_model: Player fees of $10-14 per session. The congregation takes a 20-40% share and the operator keeps the rest less host cost. Kit rental or sale ($200/month or $3-5k) and an insurance-program commission.
non_obvious_insight: The court shortage is framed as a construction problem needing $900M. It is a liability and coordination problem: the courts already exist as 40x70 ft hardwood rooms with parking, owned by institutions that want steady income but cannot underwrite risk. A congregation is also a more trusted neighbor than a new commercial club.
first_30_days: Sign 3 congregations with gyms in one metro through denominational property committees and local pickleball Facebook groups. Run two open-play nights a week using a $1.5k kit. Pre-sell via local groups, track fill rate, and get a church-insurer quote. Aim for $1-2k revenue in the first month.

title: Birth Plan B for Maternity Deserts
one_liner: Carve the last three weeks of childbirth logistics out of the hospital: pre-booked lodging, ride dispatch, nurse triage and an emergency-delivery kit for mothers whose local labor ward closed.
customer: Payers: Medicaid managed-care plans and state programs spending Rural Health Transformation money, rural employers and self-insured plans, and mothers directly ($349 to $699). Users: pregnant women in maternity-desert counties.
problem: At least 96 hospital labor-and-delivery units closed across 35 states between 2024 and early 2026, and in nearly 60% of affected counties it was the only birthing facility. About one in three US counties is a maternity-care desert, and more Medicaid cuts starting in 2027 are expected to close more units. Families improvise the final weeks: a 60 to 90 minute drive, no place to stay at 39 weeks, a partner who cannot leave work, and unplanned roadside births.
solution: A subscription from week 34. It includes choosing and pre-registering a receiving hospital, plus a contracted hotel or extended-stay room within 15 minutes of that hospital, for the 38 to 41 week window or triggered at first contractions. It adds on-call ride dispatch through a local non-emergency medical transport or taxi operator, with backup childcare and pet care. A 24/7 OB-nurse triage line (a telehealth partner) decides between go now and wait. The kit includes emergency-birth supplies and a 45-minute partner class coordinated with local EMS, and it ends with a return ride and first-week check-ins. No clinical license is needed because it wraps logistics around existing care.
why_now: CMS awarded the $50B Rural Health Transformation Program to all 50 states on December 29, 2025 (about $200M per state in year one). 35 state applications include maternal or child health, several include obstetric transport, and states face an October 30, 2026 deadline to obligate first-year awards. That makes subcontractors with a concrete pilot unusually welcome right now.
revenue_model: A per-member-per-pregnancy fee of roughly $300 to $900 from Medicaid managed-care plans as a value-added benefit, or a state RHTP subaward. Consumer self-pay of $349 to $699. Employer add-on for rural self-insured plans. Margin on lodging and rides.
non_obvious_insight: When a unit closes, the hospital's cost disappears and the family's cost explodes in the final three weeks. The fix is logistics (room blocks, dispatch, triage), which a non-clinical startup can assemble in weeks. Medicaid finances roughly four in ten US births and already pays for non-emergency transport, so the payer exists. The wedge is packaging this as a contractable benefit plans can add, with roadside-birth and ED-bypass metrics as proof.
first_30_days: Pick one closure county in the news and its receiving hospital 45 to 90 minutes away. Contract 6 discounted extended-stay rooms, one local transport operator and a telehealth OB-nurse line. Pilot with 20 mothers via the county health department, WIC and rural clinics, priced at cost or free. Log outcomes. Pitch two Medicaid plans' value-added-benefit teams and the state RHTP office with the pilot data and a one-page subaward proposal before the October 30 obligation deadline. In parallel, sell the consumer version through rural parenting groups, churches and doulas.

title: Rent Renewal Desk for Small Tenants
one_liner: Contingency-fee lease-renewal negotiation for tenants under 5,000 square feet, armed with the comps and lease abstraction that landlords get from CoStar-class data and small tenants never see.
customer: Independent restaurants, salons, clinics, small offices and shops with leases expiring in 6 to 18 months. Channels: bookkeepers and CPAs, POS providers and merchant associations.
problem: Landlords and their brokers negotiate with professional comps and lease abstracts, while small tenants negotiate blind. Tenant-rep brokers skip small deals because the commission is too small, so owners accept the renewal escalator, the personal guarantee and CAM charges by default. Crowdsourced comp platforms such as CompStak sell to brokers and investors, not to a florist with a lease renewal.
solution: The tenant uploads the lease and the last 12 months of CAM invoices. The desk builds a comp set (public deeds, listing asking rents, pooled tenant-contributed leases, licensed broker data), then returns a one-page 'you pay X% over or under market' report plus a negotiation script and draft letter. An optional we-negotiate tier uses a licensed broker partner, and a CAM audit is an upsell. Renewal alerts fire 18 months before expiry.
why_now: LLM document extraction can now abstract a 60-page lease and CAM reconciliation in minutes at a cost of cents, work that used to cost a lawyer $500 to $1,500. Tariff and wage pressure has made rent the last fixed cost small operators can still attack. CompStak's give-to-get model shows lease data can be crowdsourced when contributors get something back.
revenue_model: A $149 fair-rent report. 20% to 25% of first-year rent savings for full negotiation. 25% contingency on CAM overcharges recovered. Bookkeeper and association referral revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Information asymmetry is total at the small end, and the professionals who could close it are priced out by deal size. AI cuts the cost of a competent negotiation to a few hours. The lasting moat is a pooled, tenant-owned lease database, because landlords' data is proprietary but tenants' data is scattered and freely contributed if they get their own comps back.
first_30_days: Offer a free fair-rent check to 50 businesses in one dense commercial corridor through two local bookkeepers and a merchants' association. Build the lease-abstraction pipeline and a first comp set from the leases collected. Close five contingency negotiations, measure realized savings, and use the results as the sales deck for the next 100 tenants.

title: Gig Social-Security Compliance Engine for Mid-Size Platforms
one_liner: A four-week compliance package for India's long tail of aggregator platforms that cannot build labour-code tooling in-house.
customer: Indian home-services, logistics, ride and staffing platforms with 5k-100k gig workers.
problem: India's labour codes require aggregator contributions to a social security fund and worker registration. Over 20% of gig workers log 70+ hours a week, and the government forced platforms to drop 10-minute branding in Jan 2026. Founders bear the audit exposure.
solution: e-Shram registration sync, contribution computation, hours-worked flags and worker benefit statements. The wedge is a fixed-fee readiness audit and setup for logistics and home-service platforms.
why_now: Labour codes are now in force, enforcement is starting, and quick-commerce attrition (51% at Zepto) pushes platforms to show worker-welfare records.
revenue_model: Rs 10-30 per worker per month plus a setup fee.
non_obvious_insight: Large platforms build in-house. The 500 mid-size platforms cannot, and they have real budgets because penalties land on founders.
first_30_days: Run free readiness audits for 10 platforms and refine the contribution calculation with a labour-law firm partner.

title: Payroll and Tax-Prep Rails for Scholarship Credit
one_liner: Embeddable 'route my credit' flows in payroll, CPA and banking tools that turn the federal scholarship tax credit into a mass-market donation default.
customer: Scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs) that need small donors and pay per gift; distribution partners such as payroll platforms, PEOs, credit unions and CPA firms take a revenue share.
problem: The credit (capped at $1,700 per donor) starts in 2027 and 31 states have opted in. Estimates run $25-50B a year, but 40% of adults have not heard of it and Treasury rules are still under White House review. Many SGOs are brand new and know how to court large donors, not tens of millions of ordinary taxpayers.
solution: A white-label widget and API: check state eligibility, choose an SGO, set up a one-tap payroll deduction or card gift, auto-generate the receipt for tax filing, track pledges and send reminders. SGOs get a dashboard of pledges and cost per donor. Launch with CPA year-end planning and one payroll or PEO partner.
why_now: The credit starts in 2027, and payroll elections and year-end tax planning in Q4 2026 are the first place defaults get set. Rules are unresolved, so a compliant routing layer gets designed into workflows now.
revenue_model: 2-4% of routed gifts paid by SGOs, or a flat per-donor fee, plus revenue share to payroll and CPA partners.
non_obvious_insight: Because the credit offsets tax owed, the barrier is not generosity but awareness and friction. Whoever owns the default placement where tax decisions happen, in payroll elections and CPA offices, captures the flow, much as workplace-giving platforms did for charity.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 SGOs in an opted-in state, including one new community-foundation SGO. Build a one-page pledge flow and a receipt generator. Approach 20 CPAs and one small payroll or PEO provider. Run a Q4 pledge drive built as pledge now, fulfill in 2027, and stay flexible until final Treasury rules.

title: Contrast Capture: Recovering Iodine From Post-Scan Urine
angle: Pairing 1: Healthcare delivery (imaging) x Critical materials/waste
one_liner: Capture iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents from patients' urine at CT and MRI centers, funded by the drug makers who now owe EU wastewater EPR fees, and recover the iodine and gadolinium.
customer: Contrast-media producers and their EPR schemes (the payer), imaging centers and hospital radiology departments (the host), and water utilities. Start in the Netherlands, Germany, the Nordics and Switzerland.
problem: Contrast agents are excreted almost entirely unchanged within about a day, pass through conventional wastewater treatment, and show up in rivers and drinking water (anthropogenic gadolinium anomalies are documented near large cities). The recast EU Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive now requires pharma and cosmetics producers to fund at least 80% of quaternary treatment costs. Treating a whole city's effluent for one class of molecule is expensive and contrast agents are very persistent. Meanwhile iodine (tens of grams per contrast CT) and the rare earth gadolinium are supply-concentrated materials being flushed away.
solution: At-source capture in radiology: single-use polymer-lined urine bags or urine-diverting toilets in the imaging suite, handed out at check-out with a prepaid courier or bin for the first voids. A central facility recovers iodine and gadolinium by ion exchange and crystallization and returns them to producers as recycled input. The product sold to producers is 'verified kilograms of contrast removed from the water cycle', a metric their EPR schemes can count against fees. Hospitals get a 'green radiology' certification.
why_now: The recast UWWTD (Directive 2024/3019) is in force and producers are beginning to work out how to meet the 80% cost share, so source-control measures are being sought now. Rare-earth and critical-materials recovery is politically fashionable, giving hospitals and funders a second reason to say yes.
revenue_model: Per-patient capture fee paid by producers or their EPR fund (a few euros per scan), plus sale of recovered iodine and gadolinium (worth roughly $1-3 of iodine per contrast CT, so it supplements rather than carries the business), plus utility co-funding contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The materials are worth pennies to a few dollars per patient; the real revenue is the avoided cost of tertiary and quaternary treatment plants, and the party who owes it is not the hospital but the drug companies. A waste business with a pharma-industry payer.
first_30_days: Sign letters of intent with two imaging centers and one water utility in the Netherlands or Germany. Run a 200-patient pilot with off-the-shelf urine bags and a university lab to measure capture rates and patient compliance. Present the data to the producers' trade body and to the EPR scheme designers as a candidate 'innovative measure' needing pilot funding.

title: Clinic-Sponsored Tuition for Loan-Capped PT Students
one_liner: Sports-medicine PT and athletic-training employers fund tuition for students shut out of federal loans, in return for a structured work commitment.
customer: Multi-site outpatient orthopedic and sports PT groups, performance-rehab clinics and athletic-training staffing contractors pay the fee. The beneficiaries are DPT and athletic-training students facing the new loan caps.
problem: Since July 1, 2026, grad loans are capped at $20.5k a year and $100k total, and PT, OT, nursing and counseling were left out of the 'professional' tier ($50k a year, $200k total). A $100-150k DPT can no longer be financed federally. Private lenders are tightening, some loans reach 16% APR, and disbursements ran up to 6 weeks late. Meanwhile clinics have chronic PT vacancies and pay recruiters roughly 15-25% of first-year salary per hire.
solution: A sponsored-seat platform. The clinic pledges tuition support paid directly to the school, using tax-free employer educational assistance (up to $5,250 a year under Section 127) plus scholarship funds. The student signs a transparent 3-year post-licensure commitment with pro-rated forgiveness, structured around state limits on stay-or-pay clauses. We handle matching, contracts, compliance and servicing. Any remaining gap routes to a CDFI or credit-union partner that underwrites on the employer's offer.
why_now: The caps went live with the fall 2026 semester, so the first affected cohorts are hitting the gap now. A healthcare-association lawsuit (suspension deadline December 2026) adds uncertainty, so students and programs want a hedge whichever way it goes. Recruiting costs are high, and the tax-free employer student-loan-repayment exclusion was made permanent in 2025.
revenue_model: A success fee of 8-12% of first-year salary (about $9-13k per seat), below the recruiter benchmark: one third at contract signing, the rest at licensure start. Plus a servicing fee of 0.5-1% on managed balances and a referral fee from the partner lender.
non_obvious_insight: Federal caps have made employers the only underwriter that can price DPT risk, because salary, licensure pass rates and vacancy cost are all known. For a clinic group, tuition-for-service is a cheaper and stickier recruiting channel than a 20% recruiter fee. It also locks in local talent in the years when the pipeline shrinks.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 PT-group owners through APTA state chapters and practice-owner communities. Sign 10 sponsored seats for the Jan/Aug 2027 cohorts. Ask 3-4 DPT programs' financial-aid offices to introduce enrolled students with funding gaps. Use a counsel-drafted contract template. No lending is needed at first; the launch product is a paid placement plus a contract.

title: Civil-Document Runners for Immigrant Families
one_liner: A vetted in-country network that retrieves, verifies and delivers birth, marriage, police and court records for consular and NVC cases, with chain-of-custody proof and no forged shortcuts.
customer: Immigration law firms and family-based petitioners (largely South Asian, Filipino, West African and Latin American communities) who pay $150-450 per document, plus rush fees and bundled certified translation and apostille.
problem: Applicants wait on USCIS, but the delays that lawyers dread most sit at the National Visa Center and consulate: 'documentarily qualified' rejections, requests for secondary evidence, and 221(g) refusals for a missing or irregular civil document. Every country issues records differently, and the State Department's reciprocity schedule is only a starting point. Families hire fixers or relatives, sometimes receive forged or improperly obtained records, and then face a permanent fraud bar (INA 212(a)(6)(C)). Lawyers keep private lists of trusted runners abroad. They cannot scale and are not available to families without counsel.
solution: A managed marketplace of vetted local partners (lawyers, licensed document agents, registry liaisons) in 8-10 high-volume corridors (India, Philippines, Mexico, Dominican Republic, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Nigeria, Vietnam, El Salvador, Haiti). Each order starts with a pre-check against the consulate's actual document list, then a tracked retrieval from the issuing office with receipt and photo proof, an 'authenticity file' documenting exactly how the record was obtained, and delivery bundled with certified translation, apostille where applicable, and secondary-evidence packets when a record truly doesn't exist. Use online registries (India DigiLocker, Philippines PSA, Mexico's online actas) wherever possible so that most orders need little or no physical runner.
why_now: Consular processing has become slower and more discretionary, with more document-authenticity scrutiny, more public-charge-related evidence demands, and periodic pauses or holds by nationality. Errors that used to cost weeks now cost months. Many civil registries have digitized since 2020, so remote retrieval is now feasible for a meaningful share of documents, which makes a thin-margin logistics business viable for a small team.
revenue_model: Per-document fee ($150-450 depending on country and rush), roughly 40-50% gross margin after local partner costs, plus bundled translation and apostille, and a subscription tier for firms that order 20 or more documents a month.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody thinks of immigration as a logistics problem, so VCs fund form software while the real bottleneck is a birth certificate in a district registry that doesn't respond to email. The valuable asset is not software but a scorecard of which local partners and registry offices actually deliver on time and produce documents consulates accept. Reliability data by country and office can be built only by handling volume, and that is a moat lawyers already acknowledge privately.
first_30_days: Pick three corridors (Philippines, Mexico, India) where much of the retrieval can be done through official online portals plus one local partner. Sign 2 partners per corridor and pilot with 5 family-immigration firms at a flat price per document. Handle every order by hand, log time-to-delivery and rejection rates by office, and publish a country-by-country reliability guide to attract the next firms.

title: Legal Hold and Discovery for Agent Traces
one_liner: Custodian mapping, hold notices and defensible export for the agent logs that are becoming the new email in litigation.
customer: Litigation-support teams at mid-size law firms and corporate legal-ops or GC teams at companies running agents, with boutique e-discovery providers as a channel.
problem: Agent traces (prompts, tool calls, retrievals, memory) sit in observability tools and vendor consoles with retention defaults of days to weeks. They are not on custodian charts, and at least one court has treated AI-generated content as discoverable, exposing parties to Rule 37(e) spoliation sanctions. EDRM and law-firm alerts in mid-2026 say agent logs become evidence when agents fail, but nobody sells the plumbing.
solution: Connectors to Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry and S3 stores, agent platform APIs and cloud logs. They inventory where traces live, generate agent custodian maps, flag legal holds and suspend deletion where APIs allow, snapshot with hash chains, redact PII and privileged material, and export to Relativity, Everlaw or Reveal. Add hold-aware deletion to reconcile GDPR erasure requests with active holds, and a Rule 26(f) checklist.
why_now: Agents moved into production across 2026, and the discovery literature has just started addressing agent traces. Observability vendors optimized for developer debugging (short retention, cheap storage), which is the opposite of what litigation needs.
revenue_model: $2-10k per matter plus $1-3k/month per connected source, with revenue share for e-discovery channel partners.
non_obvious_insight: E-discovery vendors will need new data sources the way they needed Slack and Teams connectors. Whoever owns the connectors to agent trace stores becomes the toll gate, and forensics tools that reconstruct incidents are not litigation-grade preservation.
first_30_days: Build 3 connectors (Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry/S3) and a one-page hold notice and agent custodian questionnaire. Recruit 3 boutique litigation-support firms as pilots and sell a $5k agent ESI readiness assessment to GCs.

title: Widow's First 90 Days, Sold Through Funeral Homes
one_liner: The pharmacy sees a death first, because refills stop. Package a pharmacist-led medicine cleanup and 90-day check-in program for the surviving spouse, and sell it to funeral homes as their aftercare offering.
customer: Independent funeral homes, which pay $95-195 per family or fold it into a package. Also out-of-town adult children, who pay $29-49 a month for someone local to watch over the surviving parent. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs.
problem: When one spouse dies, the survivor often loses the person who managed the pillbox for both. The survivor skips or double-doses their own meds. The decedent's opioids and benzodiazepines sit in the house, where they can be diverted or swallowed by a grandchild. The first months after spousal loss carry a well-documented spike in illness and mortality, yet the funeral home hands over a grief booklet and the family scatters. No institution owns the medicine cabinet.
solution: A 'Steady' kit enrolled at the arrangement conference with one text. Within a week the pharmacist collects, counts and safely disposes of the decedent's meds, using the pharmacy's DEA-authorized collector status, which funeral homes lack. The pharmacist reconciles the survivor's own meds, resets med sync with adherence packaging and delivery, and flags deprescribing candidates for the doctor. Then come structured 30/60/90-day calls covering eating, sleeping, mood, falls and missed doses, with a report to the adult child and referrals to grief support or the physician when flags trip.
why_now: The first baby boomers turn 80 in 2026, so deaths in the 75-90 cohort will climb for two decades. Small funeral homes are squeezed by cremation and consolidators and need a differentiator beyond price. Independent pharmacies need new cash services as PBM margins collapse. Startups like Empathy have shown that families, employers and insurers pay for post-death help, but none touch medicines. Opioid-settlement money is funding take-back and safe disposal.
revenue_model: Funeral home pays per enrolled family, or the fee is folded into a package uplift. Families or adult children pay a subscription for the 90-day check-in service. The pharmacy earns on med sync, delivery and adherence packaging, plus MTM comprehensive medication review fees. Later, Medicare Advantage plans and PACE programs pay for bereavement-risk outreach.
non_obvious_insight: A pharmacist learns of a death before the obituary runs, because the refill pattern stops and the survivor's profile changes. The pharmacist and the funeral director are the two professionals in every small town who deal with aging and dying. They have never shared a channel, and a disposal-authorized pharmacist is the only one who can legally take the leftover controlled drugs.
first_30_days: One pharmacy owner recruits two funeral homes in the same county. Build a one-page kit with a DEA-compliant collection procedure, a survivor med review checklist, a med-sync reset and a 30/60/90 call script. Pilot with 20 families, free to the funeral home at first, then $95 per family. Track bottles collected, discrepancies found and 90-day ER visits. Present the case study at the state funeral directors' association meeting and line up an MTM platform partner to bill the comprehensive medication reviews.

title: Sponsor-Paid Care Network for Canine Trials
angle: Pairing 2: Biotech tools/synbio/lab automation/AI drug discovery x Pets & animal health/vet shortage/pet insurance
one_liner: Biotechs pay for dogs' cancer care in exchange for clean, immune-competent efficacy data, solving pet-owner affordability and drug-developer validation at once.
customer: Clinical-stage biotechs (including AI-drug-discovery companies) and animal-health developers that need cheap in vivo efficacy and safety signals pay per enrolled dog. General-practice and specialty clinics are site partners. Foundations can co-fund.
problem: 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and about 80% of dogs with lymphoma never receive IV chemo. On the other side, AI-designed drugs are bottlenecked by assays and validation, mouse models predict poorly, and FDA's Sept 21, 2026 rule makes sponsors show that non-animal methods are 'adequately validated'. Spontaneous tumors in pet dogs (lymphoma, osteosarcoma, mast cell, bladder cancer) are well-established human-relevant models, yet trials struggle to recruit because the dogs are first seen in general practices.
solution: A network of 30-60 general practices plus a few specialty centers. AI trial-matching runs over practice-management data and an owner-facing trial finder. Sponsors fund a standard-of-care baseline (diagnostics and supportive care) so owners get treatment free. The studio handles owner consent, GCP-style data capture, INAD/CVM paperwork, and opt-in blood and tissue banking. Start with observational registries and PK/PD window studies of oral and repurposed generic drugs, then move to sponsor-funded interventional studies.
why_now: AI-biotech funding is over $6B in 2026 and sponsors are hunting for validation evidence. FDA's Sept 2026 rule and its 25-use-case NAM database push developers away from lab animals without banning them. Duffield ($250M) and PetSmart Charities are funding 'access to care', so grant co-funding for clinics is available. Oral options like Laverdia now make community-level oncology treatable.
revenue_model: $15-30k per enrolled dog (treatment, site fees, monitoring, data), at roughly 30% gross margin. $100-250k per observational registry or PK window study. Foundation grants subsidize owner-side costs.
non_obvious_insight: Pet trials fail on recruitment and owner cost, not on science. The general-practice vet is where 90% of cases first appear, and no one connects them to sponsors. Turning a sponsor's development budget into owners' treatment budgets solves the affordability crisis and delivers a data product for drug developers.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 clinics and one board-certified oncologist as scientific lead. Pitch 10 biotechs on a $100-200k canine lymphoma real-world-outcomes registry or a dog PK window study of a repurposed oral drug. Co-apply for a foundation grant to cover owner costs. Keep the first studies observational or extra-label to stay clear of the heavier INAD requirements. First revenue in about 4-6 months.

title: Peak-Season Exchange for Idle Warehouse Robot Hours
one_liner: A marketplace and price index that moves idle AMRs and robots-as-a-service capacity between 3PLs and retailers to cover seasonal peaks, priced per robot-hour.
customer: Mid-size 3PLs and retailers needing Q4 peak capacity, and owners of idle fleets (integrators, RaaS providers, seasonal retailers, lenders holding repossessed units). Lenders and investors buy the index.
problem: Peaks force 3PLs into premium temp labor, while fleets sized for average load sit idle for half the year at seasonal operators. There is no market price for a robot-hour, so lenders cannot value the assets either.
solution: Standardize robot-hour listings (AMR class, payload, WMS integration) with a 48-hour commissioning kit (mapping, WMS connector) and escrowed insurance. Seed supply from idle demo pools and seasonal owners, and publish a weekly Robot Rate Index by class and region. Add forward contracts for peak later.
why_now: Robot pricing is becoming public and recurring (Figure's planned $600 a month lease, 1X at $499 a month, Agility's $300M+ order), and buyers want outcome pricing and 48-hour product-mix changes. Peak season 2026 is starting now, so the first rentals can be tested against real labor premiums.
revenue_model: 12-18% take rate on rentals, a commissioning fee per deployment, and $10-30k a year for index and benchmark subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Robots are sold as capex but bought as capacity. Once tens of thousands of units exist, capacity will trade like trailers and rail cars, and whoever runs the exchange sets the price benchmark (DAT, Drewry) and owns residual-value data.
first_30_days: Source about 50 idle AMRs from 2 integrators' demo pools and 2 seasonal retailers. Sell 3 emergency Q4 peak rentals to 3PLs paying temp-labor premiums, and publish Robot Rate Index v0 from about 40 collected quotes.

title: Cinemas and Arcades as Paid Heat Refuges
angle: Pairing 1: Climate adaptation x Gaming/entertainment/live experiences/fandoms
one_liner: A standby network of independent cinemas, bowling alleys, arcades and LAN centers that counties activate on heat and smoke days and pay per verified visit.
customer: County and city heat or emergency-management offices, starting with one that has a heat-action plan and a live indoor-temperature mandate (LA County, Maryland counties). Landlords of buildings under indoor temperature caps are the second buyer.
problem: Cooling centers are libraries and rec centers with short hours. Seniors, night-shift workers and teens do not go. Cooling is now a legal duty for landlords: Maryland 80F cap since June 2026, LA County 82F from Jan 2027, NYC 78F from 2030 (secondary sources). When a chiller fails, the fallback is hotel rooms at $150+ a night. Meanwhile independent cinemas, bowling alleys and family entertainment centers sit half-empty on weekday afternoons, with HVAC sized for 300 people.
solution: Pre-contract 20-60 venues per county under a standby agreement. A heat trigger (heat index or WBGT threshold) or smoke trigger (AQI above 150) activates them. On activation, venues open a free-entry lane with water, a screening and a quiet room. Outreach goes out by 211, SMS and health-plan lists, and QR or phone check-in creates per-visit proof. The county pays a standby fee plus a per-verified-visit-hour fee. Landlords can buy prepaid outage passes for tenants when their cooling fails.
why_now: Summer 2026 was reported as the hottest US July on record, and the European heatwave death toll shifted political attention. Cooling mandates are arriving on a 2027-2032 phase-in, so demand is scheduled, not random. FEMA's BRIC money was cancelled, court-restored and then closed to applications on Jul 23 2026, so cities need cheap opex solutions rather than built capacity. Venues want non-ticket revenue.
revenue_model: $150-400 standby fee per venue per heat season, plus $8-15 per verified visit-hour paid by the county. The platform keeps about 25%. Landlord outage passes at $10-15 per tenant-day. Venues keep concession sales.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in a heat emergency is not cold air. It is willingness to go somewhere and stay for six hours. Entertainment venues are dwell-time machines that already hold 300 people at 70F with a reason to stay. Paying only for activated days flips cooling centers from capex to opex with zero idle capacity, and smoke days come free because cinemas can run high-grade filtration.
first_30_days: Pick one county with a heat-action plan and a 2027 budget cycle. Sign LOIs from 5-8 owner-operated cinemas, bowling alleys and arcade bars (phone calls, not enterprise sales). Run an unpaid test activation on the next warm spell or smoke day. Write a one-page cost comparison against hotel vouchers and take it to the county emergency office, one Medicaid managed-care plan and 10 property managers.

title: Skill Rooms: Proctored Work-Sample Studios for Hiring
one_liner: Walk-in, device-free testing studios where candidates take a 90-minute employer-designed work sample under ID-verified proctoring, with a portable score that many employers honor.
customer: Staffing firms and mid-size employers hiring entry and mid-level roles (customer support, analysts, junior developers, paralegals, sales development) who are drowning in AI-written applications and AI-assisted interview cheating. Employers pay $75-200 per sitting, candidates pay nothing.
problem: Resumes and cover letters are now noise. In a dataset of about 19,000 live interviews from mid-2025 to early 2026, over a third of candidates showed signs of AI-assisted cheating (close to half in software engineering). Google, Cisco and McKinsey have brought back in-person rounds, but each employer improvising its own on-site test is expensive.
solution: Studios in 10 metros, rented after hours from coworking spaces and community colleges. Fixed-time sittings with ID checks and locked-down machines, and standard job-family work samples (writing under time limit, spreadsheet modeling, code on an air-gapped machine, mock client call), scored by rubric with human review and AI assistance. Candidates get a 'Verified Work Sample' credential valid for 12 months and portable across employers, and employers receive pre-screened slates.
why_now: AI cheating in remote interviews is now measurable and widely reported, in-person verification is returning at large employers, and entry-level applicant floods make cheap, trustworthy screening valuable. Existing proctoring vendors (OnVUE and similar) focus on certification exams, not hiring work samples.
revenue_model: Per-sitting fee from employers, premium pricing for custom work samples, per-hire placement fees through staffing partners, and optional paid practice tests for candidates.
non_obvious_insight: When signals get cheap, standardized proctored tests win, which is how the SAT displaced recommendation letters. The portable score, not the room, is the business: every additional employer that honors it lowers each candidate's cost of proving skill and raises its value, and it gives displaced or credential-less workers a way to prove themselves without a degree.
first_30_days: Rent a 12-seat room in one city and sign 5 staffing agencies hiring for three roles. Design three work samples and rubrics, then run a first cohort of about 40 candidates. Charge employers $125 per candidate who passes, and use the results to sign the next 10 employers on the same score.

title: Skin-Tone-Verified SpO2 Validation Cooperative
one_liner: Build the 10x-larger, objectively skin-tone-measured, arterial-blood-paired dataset that pulse-oximeter and wearable makers need, and sell access, bias reports and validation studies.
customer: Pulse-oximeter and wearable OEMs and startups, plus hospital purchasing groups that want independent bias reports before buying devices.
problem: Current pulse oximeters tend to overestimate arterial saturation in darkly pigmented patients, so low oxygen can go undetected. A new arXiv correction method works on 98 patients from the public OpenOximetry Repository but the authors say a cohort roughly ten times larger is needed for significance. The 2013 FDA 510(k) guidance asks for only 'at least 2 darkly pigmented subjects or 15% of your subject pool' and says nothing of objective pigmentation measures.
solution: Recruit a diverse cohort and characterize each participant with a skin reflectance spectrometer to get melanin fraction. Run induced-hypoxia studies with paired arterial samples through partner university hypoxia labs. License the de-identified dataset and calibration models to OEMs, and offer per-device bias validation and a public 'bias report card' for hospital buyers.
why_now: The 2026 arXiv paper by Blaney, Fantini, Koomson and colleagues shows a melanin-aware correction that cut error from +2.8 to +0.1 percentage points per unit melanin fraction, but it is data-limited. Wearable SpO2 features are now mainstream, and regulators and buyers are asking for skin-tone-diverse evidence. I could not verify in this session the status of the January 2025 FDA draft guidance, so confirm it before pitching.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses of roughly $50-250k, per-device validation studies of $100-400k, and annual bias-report subscriptions for hospital groups and OEMs.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is data, not algorithms. The arXiv paper says current oximeters 'overestimate arterial saturation in darkly pigmented patients', its correction relies on per-patient skin-tone measurement, and 'a cohort roughly ten times larger is needed' (https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30122). The current FDA 510(k) guidance sets a low bar of 2 darkly pigmented subjects or 15% of the pool (https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/pulse-oximeters-premarket-notification-submissions-510ks-guidance-industry-and-food-and-drug). Whoever owns the largest objectively measured dataset sets the de facto standard, and every OEM has to buy or replicate it.
first_30_days: Email the arXiv authors and OpenOximetry contributors about their data needs. Sign a partner hypoxia lab and an IRB pathway, and design a 30-50 participant pilot. Pre-sell the pilot dataset to 3 wearable or oximeter startups through LOIs. Prototype a spectrometer-based melanin measurement protocol and publish a pre-registered study plan.

title: Repair-Rights Compliance Portal in a Box
one_liner: A hosted repair.yourbrand.com that publishes the parts lists, manuals, pricing and order forms that US state and EU repair laws require, plus the rules engine and audit trail behind it.
customer: Compliance, legal and customer-service leads at mid-market consumer-electronics, appliance, e-bike, power-tool and mobility brands ($30M-$1B revenue) selling in Washington, Texas, Oregon and the EU. Retailers are a second segment.
problem: Washington's law took effect 1 Jan 2026, Texas applies from Sep 2026 to electronics over $50, Oregon bans parts pairing, the EU directive's transposition deadline was 31 Jul 2026, and an EU repair platform is due 1 Jan 2028. Each regime differs in scope, dates and price rules, and the briefing found nobody selling compliance tooling for repair-information forms or parts-availability tracking.
solution: Portal templates and connectors: product-catalog import, SKU mapping to state or EU scope and effective dates, auto-published manuals and parts lists, a parts order form with a fair-price check, pairing-policy disclosures, an SLA timer and request log for regulators, and an EU repair-information-form generator. Regulatory updates ship as configuration changes.
why_now: Multiple obligations hit in the past nine months (Washington Jan 2026, EU transposition Jul 2026, Texas Sep 2026) and Oregon dates are still unclear in public sources, so brands cannot rely on a single law-firm memo.
revenue_model: $15-60k/year per brand by SKU count, $10-30k implementation, and a per-order fee on parts sales.
non_obvious_insight: The core burden of repair law is publication and response time, which is CMS and workflow work, not legal analysis. Law firms bill hourly for what is really a web app, and the portal also cuts support costs.
first_30_days: Pick 30 mid-market brands with Texas exposure from product listings and email compliance leads a free one-page 'Texas gap audit'. Build a minimal portal for three design partners at a $5k pilot fee.
